text:
In late August 1854, a terrible illness struck the crowded streets of Soho, in London. Cholera, a disease that causes violent vomiting and diarrhea and can kill a healthy adult within a day or two, had visited England before. But few neighborhoods had suffered as quickly as the ones around Broad Street. Within about ten days, more than five hundred people living within a few hundred yards of one another had died. Many families fled. Shops closed. The district fell silent.

At the time, nearly everyone believed that cholera spread through bad air. This idea was called the miasma theory. Foul smells rising from rotting garbage, sewers and the river were thought to carry poison that people breathed in. The theory was not foolish. Dirty neighborhoods really did have more disease, and the smell of London in the 1850s was famously awful. But it was wrong, and acting on it could not stop the deaths.

John Snow, a physician living in Soho, had a different suspicion. He was a respected doctor who had pioneered the use of anesthesia, and he had given chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth. He had also been thinking about cholera for years. In 1849 he had published a short essay arguing that the disease was carried in contaminated water and swallowed, not breathed. His reasoning was simple. Cholera attacked the gut first, not the lungs. Something that made people sick in the stomach, he argued, was more likely to have been eaten or drunk. Most doctors were unconvinced.

The Broad Street outbreak gave Snow a chance to test his idea. He knew the neighborhood and he knew many of the families. He began going door to door, asking who had fallen ill, where they lived and, crucially, where they got their drinking water. In those days, most homes had no running taps. People collected water from public pumps in the street, and the water came from different companies and different sources. One pump stood at the corner of Broad Street and Cambridge Street.

Snow also obtained the official list of deaths from the local registrar and began marking each address on a map of the neighborhood. A small black bar represented each death, stacked at the house where it occurred. As the map filled in, a pattern appeared. The bars clustered thickly around the Broad Street pump. The farther one moved from it, the fewer the deaths.

Pattern alone was not proof, and Snow knew it. A skeptic could say the area was simply poor and crowded. So he looked for exceptions, the cases that did not fit. Near the pump stood a workhouse, a large institution housing about five hundred poor residents, yet only a handful had died. Snow discovered the workhouse had its own well, so its residents did not use the Broad Street pump. A brewery on the nearby street employed seventy workers, and none of them died. The men were given free beer as part of their pay, and the brewery also had its own well. They seem to have had little reason to drink from the pump.

Then there were the strange cases from far away. A widow living in Hampstead, several miles north, died of cholera. Snow learned that she had once lived in Soho and loved the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had a bottle of it carried to her each day. Her niece, who visited her and drank some, also died. Nobody else in her neighborhood fell ill.

By early September, Snow was convinced. On the evening of September 7, he went to a meeting of the local board of guardians and presented his evidence. He urged them to remove the pump handle, so no one could draw water from it. The officials were skeptical, but the case was strong enough that they agreed. The next day the handle was taken off. The pump went dead.

The story is often told as though removing the handle ended the epidemic at a stroke. The truth is less tidy. The outbreak had already been fading, partly because so many residents had fled and partly because the sickest had already died. Snow himself admitted that the decline might have begun before the handle was removed. Even so, his investigation was one of the first times anyone had used careful counting, mapping and questioning to trace a disease to its source.

Later inquiry found a likely culprit. A cesspool lay close to the well, and the clergyman Henry Whitehead, who had at first doubted Snow, discovered that a baby in a nearby house had died of a diarrheal illness just before the outbreak. Its soiled diapers had been washed into the cesspool, and waste had seeped through the brickwork into the well water. Whitehead became a convert and helped Snow refine the evidence.

Official bodies still resisted. Snow died in 1858, aged forty-five, with the miasma theory still dominant. Only in later decades, after the discovery of bacteria, was his view fully vindicated. Today he is remembered as a founder of modern epidemiology, the study of how diseases spread through populations.
